pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/kamapuaa/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**kamapuaa** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Kamapuaa.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Kamapuaa" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Kamapuaa" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"kamapuaa" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Kamapuaa ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Kamapuaa ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Kamapuaa ‌place ​pig god, ​agriculture ​at the ​center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### Origins ‌(Myth)

​Kamapuaa appears ‌in ​polynesian ‌tradition as ​pig ​god, agriculture. ​The ​name's ​meaning, "male ‌fertility ​deity in ‌Hawaiian ​mythology", ‌shapes the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

Devotees ‌and ‌later tradition-keepers ​preserved ​Kamapuaa ‌in ritual, ​text, ​and iconography, ‌ensuring ​the ​name survived ‌into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

​The myths ​of ​Kamapuaa survive ‌in ‌fragments, ​summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. Each ​version ‌reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ​— ‌poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ‌PuniCodex ​entry does ​not ​privilege ‌a single ​version; ​it gathers ​the ‌attestations ​so that ‌readers ​can compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Kamapuaa ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

archaeology.body:

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming Kamapuaa, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to pig ​god ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Kamapuaa** ​(*kamapuaa*) — ‌Pig ‌God, Agriculture ​· male ​fertility ​deity in ​Hawaiian ​mythology — ‌belongs to ​the ​Polynesian tradition, ‌where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Pig ​God, ​Agriculture". The ​name ​means "male ​fertility ‌deity in ​Hawaiian mythology"[^1].

‌**Kamapua'a** ​is the ‌pig-god ​of O'ahu ‌— **shape-shifter, ​ravager ‌of plantations, ​master ​of rain ‌and ‌flood**, and ‌the only ​suitor ​who ever ‌beat ​Pele at ​her ‌own element. ​He is ​agriculture's ‌wild side: ​the ‌animal that ​roots up ​the ​garden, and ​the ‌storm that ‌waters ​it.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records the ​canonical ​scholarly spelling ‌**Kamapuaa** ‌and serves ‌its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/kamapuaa/). ‌The ​displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The ​plain ASCII ​form *kamapuaa* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in modern ​Polynesian ​orthographies; macron ​usage ​follows each ​tradition’s ‌reference dictionaries. ​Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"male ‌fertility deity ​in ‌Hawaiian mythology"[^1].

​The ​canonical spelling ​**Kamapuaa** ​matches the ​conventional ‌scholarly romanization. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ‌*kamapuaa* contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ‌no lost ​diacritics ​or encoding ‌transition ‌is ‌claimed. The ​editorial ​work is ‌to ​fix one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ‌provenance, ​and keep ‌the ​original evidence ​visible. ​The displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ‌computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ‌itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ​**k** ‌→ **K** ​— ​Same, capitalized
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ​Same
- **m** ​→ ‌**m** — ​Same
- ​**a** → ​**a** ‌— Same
- ​**p** ‌→ **p** ​— ‌Same
- ​**u** → ‌**u** ‌— Same
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ​— ​Same
- **a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

meditation.body:
Every ​agricultural people ‌knows the ‌animal in ​Kamapua'a: the ​creature that ​is wealth ​and destruction ​in one ‌body — ​the pig ​that manures ‌the field ​and roots ‌it up, ​the rain ‌that drowns ​the seedlings ​and ​fills the ​pond. What ​Hawaiian myth ‌did with ​that knowledge ‌is marry ​it. The ‌boar does ​not get ‌exterminated in ​this cycle; ‌he gets ​**married to ​the volcano** ‌and bound ‌by treaty. ‌It ​is among ​the most ‌sophisticated land-use ​stories in ​this catalog: ‌destruction domesticated ​not by ​force but ‌by alliance, ​the pest ‌made a ​spouse with ​terms.

There ​is a ​gentler reading ‌too. Kamapua'a ‌is the ​child ‌no one ​wanted — ​half pig, ‌born in ‌the least ‌approachable valley ‌on the ​island — ‌who grows ​up to ​be the ​one being ‌Pele cannot ​defeat. The ​despised form ​conceals the ‌effective ​nature. His ​cycle tells ​every misfit ‌with a ​stubborn streak ‌what the ​tradition believes: ‌you are ​not the ‌problem; you ‌are the ​untried element, ​and the ​day will ​come when ‌even the ‌volcano needs ​rain.[^1]
